You can hold the dried gourd in one hand and the wooden handle in the other, or hold the handle and shake the instrument. The usual order is to practise shaking first, so that the net naturally hits the shell; then striking, slapping the net with the palm, which handles faster and more precise rhythms but gives a shorter ring and more damping; and finally rubbing, using the fingers or palm to let the net rub against the shell for a fine, dense sound. A beginner should control wrist rotation, palm strike and rubbing force separately, and note that normally only one instrument is used.

沙克雷鼓 為體鳴樂器，乾葫蘆外覆珠網，靠搖動、拍打或摩擦珠網發聲。來源提到它流行: The shekere is an idiophone: a dried gourd covered with a net of beads, sounded by shaking, slapping or rubbing the net. The sources say it is popular in West Africa and Latin America and common in folk music and some popular music; in Ghana it is called axatse, and in Latin America often cabaça. In Cuba the chekeré is used in Afro-Cuban religious and popular music; it can be twisted, shaken or slapped, and is more flexible than a maraca. In Brazil it is called xequerê, and there is also a smaller afoxé.
謝科雷葫蘆鈴傳統琴身多用藤葫蘆，經數月曬乾後去除果肉與種子，再擦洗並加上珠工與顏: The traditional body of the shekere is usually a vine gourd, dried for several months and then scraped free of flesh and seeds, washed and finished with beadwork and colour; the sound source is a net woven of beads or shells that covers the gourd. Modern materials include plastic or carbon-fibre shells, and the net may be plastic fishing net with plastic beads, or cord netting with hand-strung beads; the Brazilian version also uses small plastic balls. Other parts include a wooden handle, in older instruments a sealed wooden handle, and there are also open-handled versions.
謝科雷葫蘆鈴源自約魯巴地區，起源於伊費王國，後在舊奧約帝國時期擴展，涵蓋奈及利亞: The shekere comes from Yorubaland, originating in the kingdom of Ife and expanding in the period of the old Oyo empire to cover Nigeria, Benin and Togo. It later spread through West Africa and to Latin America and became an important instrument in the folk music of many countries, and it appears in some popular music too. In Ghana it is called axatse, in Latin America often cabaça; Cuba calls it chekeré or aggué and uses it in Afro-Cuban religious and popular music, Brazil calls it xequerê and has a smaller afoxé as well. Modern versions also come with plastic or carbon-fibre shells and open handles.

Its sound comes from the beads striking the dried gourd, and its range is concentrated in the middle and high frequencies, with a strong sense of rhythm and carrying power. The hollow gourd resonates and amplifies the waves, giving a sound with plenty of layers: a bright shimmer in the high frequencies over a warm low foundation. Compared with a shaker, the shekere is fuller and rounder; compared with a tambourine it is softer and more natural, never sharp. Shaken, its colour is continuous and flowing; slapped against the palm, its notes are clear and distinct. The two ways of playing give different acoustic results and make the instrument expressive in many ways.

The shekere (Yoruba Ṣẹ̀kẹ̀rẹ̀, also called the calabash rattle) is an idiophone percussion instrument made from a dried gourd or calabash; the seeds and flesh are hollowed out and a net full of beads is fitted around the outside, and a handle may be added. The player shakes, slaps or rubs it: shaking the handle makes the beads strike the shell, the palm slaps the bead net, or the fingers rub beads against the shell. It comes from Yorubaland in West Africa and is played in West Africa and Latin America, often in folk music and popular music, as well as in Afro-Cuban religious and popular music.
